# Why the Cyberpocalypse Might Hit China Harder

### The geopolitics of disclosure norms and hacker incentives

Chang Che is a writer and contributor to the New Yorker .

In August, researchers at a California security firm used an OpenAI model to find a software bug in PHP, a programming language that undergird some seventy per cent of the world’s websites, including Wikipedia and WordPress. They alerted PHP’s developers, who quietly began working on a fix. By late October, the fix was ready, but before they could alert the world, the break-in attempts had begun. Days earlier, Amazon detected someone trying to hack into its servers; attacks code began circulating online. Some governments and companies began pulling websites down, rather than risk a security breach. One security firm described the flaws as some of the worst ever found in PHP, “and arguably in software history.”

Before AI, the internet might have looked, to a hacker, like a worn-out bug screen. You could discern some holes with a keen eye, and that knowledge was reliably asymmetric—others probably didn’t know about the holes you found. Moreover, tunneling through the holes undetected took months or years of human labor, talent, and money. Now, with AI, the internet looks more like a block of Swiss cheese: the holes are obvious, anyone can, or will, see them, and the time and cost it takes to exploit these software flaws have plunged alarmingly fast . According to Google’s incident response team , the average time it takes for cyber criminals to exploit a new vulnerability is -7 days, meaning hacking attempts are “routinely occurring before a patch is even released.”

Hackers refer to unbeknownst software bugs like PHP as “zero-days” because a defender has had zero days to protect themselves upon its discovery. Once a hacker discovers a zero-day in, say, iOS software, every iPhone user is potentially vulnerable to a hack until Apple finds out about it, fixes it, releases a new patch, and, crucially, gets customers to install the software update. Beyond losing your crypto-wallets, there is the question of what the cyberpocalypse means, strategically, for the United States and China. According to the data tracking site Censys , the two countries reacted at drastically different speeds to the PHP zero-day. One week after its public disclosure, the United States had successfully patched over a quarter of the 14 million services exposed to the flaw. (Japan had about the same percentage.) China, by contrast, had patched an abysmal 4% of its potentially vulnerable services.

Why was China, who spent a decade building up a formidable cybersecurity governance system, so slow to patch one of the biggest software flaws in history? Until now, the cybersecurity industry was largely built around finding flaws. Companies buy them from hackers, and governments hoard them to spy on their enemies. An industry built around bug-discovery seems to resemble the AI race or the Manhattan Project: it’s a question of how a state can marshall a small elite group toward a specific goal. China is very good at the former—as it has repeatedly demonstrated with AI, semiconductors, batteries, robotics.

We are now moving from an era of zero-day scarcity to zero-day abundance. Bugs that Washington, Moscow, and Beijing used to hoard like nuclear fission material are now becoming available to an educated AI user. An era of zero-day abundance will force cybersecurity to shift to an industry built around fixing flaws as fast as humanly, or superhumanly, possible. This is a challenge for the many, not the few—it demands something from your average IT person at a school, the contractor running a local water plant, a security team at a tech firm whose warnings may have previously been ignored. It’s almost a test of the metabolism of a society: how well bottom-up incentives are working. China, with its Leninist governance system, may have trouble in an era that demands such uncoordinated, yet collective, actions.

# Hayek and the birth of disclosure norms

“Zero-days,” unlike proofs, can be weaponized, and in the 1990s, there were practically no rules for what one should do with the ingredients of a potential cyber-nuke. “White hat” hackers—people who hack to help shore up defenses—who told companies about their flaws were often ignored, bullied, or threatened with lawsuits. So hackers began posting the flaws publicly. This forced companies to fix them, but it also handed “black hat” hackers the cyber equivalent of a bank’s blueprint, so a deal had to be brokered. Entire books have been written about the battle between the hacker community and tech companies, but the upshot was that by the 2010s, an equilibrium solidified. Under the rules of “coordinated vulnerability disclosure,” a researcher notifies the affected company first, gives them time to fix it, then tells the world.

Today, a web of institutions and standards, anchored in the United States, underwrite these norms. Google’s Project Zero, an elite bug-hunting team, gives software makers 90 days to fix a flaw before it goes public. The “bug bounty” program, which Netscape pioneered in 1995, went from a quirky experiment to an industry standard that can pay hackers six figures for a single flaw. Serious bugs get an ID number from CVE, a catalog run by the US government. What’s striking is that no one designed this system from the top-down. It more closely resembled Friedrich Hayek’s theory of “ spontaneous order ”: free, commercially motivated groups—hackers and companies—adjusted to each other and the rules and institutions emerged. Hackers wanted credit and rewards; firms needed time. Money supplied the incentives for a bug-patching ecology that resulted in a more secure web.

One way to measure how American this metabolic process is is to compare the maturity of bug bounty programs in other countries. Out of the ten largest tech companies in the United States, nine of them have bug bounty programs, according to a 2026 study ; in China, the number is six out of ten. (The firms that have them, like Alibaba, are international facing, while the ones that don’t are state-owned like China Mobile.) The pay scale is incomparable. Apple and Google can pay millions of dollars for critical zero-day flaws, while top Chinese programs like Tencent top out at $15,000. The West underwrites the ecosystem for patching up the internet.

# After Snowden

Of course, this state of affairs didn’t last. While the bug-disclosure norms were taking shape, there was also a parallel, secretive cyber-arms-trade going on. In This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends , published in 2021, the former New York Times cybersecurity reporter Nicole Perlroth shows how the NSA was secretly buying zero-days from hackers to spy on American citizens and the world. Hackers were paid life-changing sums to keep their flaws secret, and the exposure of this hoarding by the Snowden leaks helped break up the love affair between Chinese hackers and Western bug bounty programs.

The Snowden revelations in 2013 catalyzed China’s cybersecurity arms race . In 2014, Xi Jinping took charge of a newly empowered cybersecurity division. Beijing began to pass laws to de-Americanize China’s tech stack, and state-sponsored cyberattacks on the United States skyrocketed. Among the biggest changes China implemented was to treat zero-days like national security assets. In 2018, Chinese hackers abruptly disappeared from the international hacking contests they once dominated. Contributions by Chinese researchers to Microsoft bug bounty programs plummeted in 2020. A year later, in 2021, Beijing passed a law that prohibited Chinese security researchers from publicizing zero-day flaws or passing them to a foreign bug-broker. They can report the bug to the company that runs the software or to China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). Any company in China that learns of a flaw has 48 hours to tell the ministry.

For decades, Western tech companies and white hat hackers had created a bug-fixing ecosystem that prized openness and defense. Chinese hackers participated, not least for the money and fame, but because fixing those bugs hardly felt “western” when Chinese offices ran Windows and Chinese phones ran Android. But it’s understandable why—in light of the NSA’s resolve to enlist US tech companies as a “ backdoor ”—China felt queasy about watching their hackers patch Microsoft’s bugs.

The NSA’s security rationale had a name: “nobody but us,” or NOBUS. Deliberately keeping the internet vulnerable was acceptable, in this view, as long as no other country knew about those vulnerabilities and could exploit it. In sourcing and keeping zero-days a secret for cyberoffensive capabilities, the US government undermined the global disclosure system its own society midwifed. China’s cybersecurity laws were the response to NOBUS. The message was: “if you are going to hoard zero-days to spy on us, we’re going to do the same.” Several experts described the 2021 law to me as a “vacuum” that siphons zero-days to what researchers at the Atlantic Council , a D.C.-based think tank, found is a national database visible to China’s spy agency. The rules were put to the test less than three months later, in 2021, when an Alibaba researcher found one of the worst software flaws in a decade in a free code base maintained by the Apache Software Foundation, a US-based nonprofit. He reported it to Apache as global norms prescribe, and MIIT suspended a partnership with Alibaba as punishment.

China used the force of law to compel its hackers to replicate the NSA’s zero-day arsenal, and it seems to have worked. Perlroth told me that after the zero-day vacuum law, the number of zero-day exploits from China-linked hackers exploded. “China was using their authoritarianism and these new laws to their advantage,” she told me. “It was an incredible up-leveling.” But what it couldn’t copy well was the West’s vulnerability disclosure ecosystem, a bottom-up process that enlists the hacker community and tech companies to work together to patch bugs with relative transparency. The issue is one of incentives. None of the cybersecurity laws encourage Chinese researchers to find bugs at all. In fact, the 2021 law closes off foreign bug-brokers who pay good money, and forbids the public disclosures that bestow researchers street cred. “Chinese bug bounty platforms offer limited incentives for hackers, with rewards often being unspecified or relatively low,” a 2024 report on China’s cyber ecosystem concluded. In trying to arm itself with cyber-weapons, China undermined its own cyber-immune system.

China’s AI labs and tech giants are trapped in the early 2000s Silicon Valley mindset of “move fast and break things.” There’s too much competition, profit-margins are razor thin, and the laws are already too cumbersome to invest in such luxuries as vulnerability infrastructure and, relatedly, AI safety. The private sector is very responsive to state diktats, which has the unforeseen consequence of failing to incentivize firms to do anything beyond what is required of them. A crackdown, I believe, is too blunt a weapon for the metabolism needed to patch a constant flood of zero-day discoveries.

Now let’s return to the cyberpocalypse.

# Korea’s Stock Market Crashed $1 Trillion. What Does That Mean for the Global AI Race?

Richard Gray is an analyst who works for a foreign policy think tank in Washington, D.C.

Since 2025, South Korea’s capital markets have vacillated from the world’s best-performing to shedding more than $1 trillion in market capitalization. This volatility is a story of how Korea’s financial system overlays supply chain specialization. With Korean firms Samsung and SK hynix controlling a majority share of global memory, South Korea’s stock market functionally operates as a single, highly leveraged node within the AI financial architecture.

Two interwoven dynamics explain the convulsions of Korean capital markets and their global ramifications. The first is the Korea discount , in which Korean equities are structurally undervalued because of lagging financial development and weak corporate governance. The second is a memory discount , with each leading high-bandwidth memory (HBM) company (Micron in the U.S., SK hynix and Samsung in Korea) having depressed valuations in their respective markets.

The June-July 2026 crash rippled far beyond Korea’s borders and forewarns what may be to come in future market corrections. For Korea, its historically shallow capital markets and exposure to the memory sector — which is now facing emergent Chinese competitors — serve as overlapping pressures on its financial position. In this environment, the threat of a market correction cascading across global markets and the U.S.-China tech competition looms large.

## The Zenith: Capital Infusion

The Korean market is essentially a bet on two companies competing in the same industry.

Korea’s memory chip industry has driven exponential year-on-year growth in Korea’s capital markets. From March 2025 to June 2026, the KOSPI — Korea’s main stock index — rose 241%, adding nearly $3.3 trillion in capitalization and exceeding the total increase accumulated over the index’s 43-year history (Bloomberg).

In June 2026, SK, Samsung, and Naver announced plans to build chipmaking plants and data center facilities worth $880 billion — a sum adding up to more than 50 percent of Korea’s current annualized GDP.

The Korean AI capital boom powered these commitments. In Q1 2026, SK hynix reported a quarter-on-quarter increase in revenue of 60%, while Samsung recorded 40% revenue growth.

This concentration bleeds into the global semiconductor supply chain. As of Q2 2026, SK hynix and Samsung collectively accounted for 83 percent of the global HBM market and 63 percent of the dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) market. Micron, the closest American competitor, maintains an 18 percent market share in HBM and 24 percent in DRAM.

This domestic and international centralization is one of the clearest financial expressions of the artificial intelligence boom. Alongside SK hynix and Samsung, Micron forms a memory chip triopoly. The emergence of CXMT — a firm with deep state backing from the world’s second-largest economy — introduces risks of China moving up another value chain, accelerating production, and drawing down market pricing. Such a conversion would challenge the position of the incumbent memory players, introducing new risks of shortfalls in valuation that could spread financial contagion across the AI stack.

## The Nadir: Capital Volatility

Korea’s memory chip bet has since faltered. From June 22 to July 16, the KOSPI entered a bear market, shrinking more than a quarter and wiping out nearly $1.1 trillion in market capitalization. (CEIC) SK hynix and Samsung fell 38% and 29% over the same window. (Bloomberg)

The June-July bear market was as tied to an industry as a country. Micron’s shares fell approximately a third in the same span, while Chinese and Taiwanese semiconductor stocks also were being sold off .

As the Iran war’s reescalation put additional pressure on the Korean economy through currency pressures and rising energy costs, Korean regulators warned of chip-sector concentration as a market risk. As of July 2026, Samsung Electronics and SK hynix alone accounted for more than half of KOSPI’s total market capitalization. In contrast, the Magnificent Seven (seven highest-valued American stocks) taken together are 37.2% of the S&P500. (Morningstar)

Throughout the first half of 2026, foreign investments have flowed out of Asian equities at a record pace — with Korea among the hardest hit. In line with the KOSPI’s crash, in May and June, South Korea’s capital flight (in equities) exceeded $35 billion. On July 28, Korea’s stock market dropped more than 8% during intraday trading, the eighth instance that year. There have been at least 33 days of upticks and downturns of more than 5%.

In response to the market’s sharp decline, the Financial Services Commission (FSC) suspended sales of leveraged Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) tied to individual stocks “until market conditions stabilize,” and tripled the minimum deposit required to trade them to $20,300, effective August 5. While ETFs often are an investment vehicle that holds a broad set of assets, the ones popularized in the Korean market were tied to the performance of single stocks and acquired in high volume through loans. These ETFs let ordinary investors bet on a single company’s stock while magnifying gains and losses. After the ETFs launched in May, trading in SK hynix and Samsung and their ETFs came to dominate the entire Korean stock market, peaking at 84 percent of all volume in June.

This volatility is partially powered by South Korea’s shallow capital markets. Historically, Korea’s capital markets have been characterized by a structural undervaluation of listed enterprises known as the “Korea discount.” Financial analysis company MSCI continues to label Korea as an emerging market, citing limited convertibility of the won in the offshore currency market, excessive requirements for foreign securities, and limited investment instruments.

Korea’s comparatively low price-to-book ratio — a comparison of stock prices and a company’s net assets — introduces risks that accompany rapid capital market growth. Throughout 2025, Korea had the lowest price-to-book of any of the surveyed markets, well below Hong Kong, Malaysia, or Singapore.

Era Dabla-Norris of the International Monetary Fund argues that shallow markets with limited diversification lead to concentrated counterparty exposures, potentially increasing financial stability risks during periods of market deepening. As the KOSPI retains a globally competitive return on equity — how efficiently companies generate profits from shareholder equity — the “Korea discount” is likely driven by a combination of genuine mispricing and governance risk.

## Caveats to the Memory Momentum

Memory has become the highest revenue-generating segment in Korea’s capital market and the global semiconductor supply chain alike. According to Gartner, memory revenue is projected to surpass $1 trillion and account for more than 55 percent of all semiconductor revenue by 2027.

The value of South Korea’s DRAM exports has increased more than fivefold year-on-year (CEIC). An increase in memory demand has led to Korea’s semiconductor export volumes more than doubling in that same period.

At the same time, there is a global memory shortage. Samsung has earmarked 70% of its memory production for long-term agreements through 2030. This supply-demand imbalance is expected to become more severe through 2028 (JP Morgan). SK hynix CEO Kwak Noh-Jung has stated that the memory shortage could persist through 2030. According to JP Morgan, DRAM prices rose more than 400% from 2024 to 2026, with greater demand and long-term arrangements increasing overall memory pricing and reducing available supply.

Historically, memory has been classified as cyclical, requiring intensive capital investments. Competition was primarily on the lines of affordability as opposed to quality, with an ebb and flow in demand and downturns shrinking the number of players within the market. There is an ongoing debate on the extent to which the AI boom has reshaped the memory industry away from its cyclical nature. Unlike in the past, the market concentration among three incumbents — and CXMT as an emergent player — with the specialization and value-add of HBMs is thought to have transformed into a “ differentiated product .”

Such a proposition relies on a continued and relatively stable demand to fuel the scale of ongoing investments. While long-term contracts provide immediate stability, they will also tie the memory industry’s future to the ability to extend them. Korea’s recent memory chip manufacturing investments are intended to be operational in 2030, just as Kwak Noh-Jung predicts that the memory chip shortage may come to a close. What then?

Maintaining the balance sheets and capital access of these national champions, therefore, is a much more expansive initiative than Korean financial stability alone.

With CXMT looking to enter the HBM market, demand is not the only factor at play. On August 31, 2026, The Information reported that CXMT met its objective of producing HBM3E — the fifth-generation HBM architecture — with the intention of expanding production in 2027. This situates CXMT two generations behind SK hynix and Samsung, which have begun shipping samples of their seventh-generation HBM4E, and one generation behind Micron’s HBM4. What is unclear is Samsung and SK hynix’s timeline for mass production of HBM4E, as well as the extent to which CXMT will be able to leapfrog generations.

#### How Far Can Chinese HBM Go?

CXMT has become a growing DRAM player and emergent HBM challenger. According to Reuters, Hefei “government-linked investors” and Anhui’s “provincial government-backed entities’ stake” account for roughly half of CXMT’s ownership, with industrial subsidies and state support contributing to the firm’s rise as China’s DRAM national champion. CXMT has continued to scale its market share in DRAM, growing from 3 percent in Q1 2025 to 10 percent in Q2 2026. In its first earnings report, CXMT reported that its H1 2026 profit was $22.4 billion after sales increased by 874%. Its market cap, as of August 28, stood at 4.01 trillion Chinese yuan.

In December 2024, the Biden administration restricted the export of DRAM and HBM to Chinese end users. In less than two years, CXMT has gone from prototyping the earliest generations of HBM to only two generations behind the cutting edge. This foothold within China — which remains its immediate priority, with HBM3E shipments to Alibaba and Cambricon Technologies — has facilitated its growing share of the global market. However, as Apple considers using CXMT as a memory supplier — even as the Trump administration opposes such sourcing — the existing shortages and price hikes could position Chinese suppliers to sell to American device and data center firms. This asymmetry of CXMT’s potential access to Chinese and global markets (assuming it is not added to Commerce’s Entity List), while Micron, SK hynix, and Samsung remain blocked from the Chinese market, could eventually compress margins and increase competition.

This market landscape and historic cyclicality materialize as a “memory discount”, where memory stocks have lower forward price-earnings ratios (PE) — current share price compared with expected earnings — than other equities on their listed exchange. This is true for SK hynix and Samsung, which are lower than the surveyed Korean firms Naver, Hanwha Ocean, and Kakao, as well as for Micron, which has a similar PE ratio to SK hynix and Samsung despite the U.S. having significantly deeper capital markets.

Of the memory players, the only current exception to this is CXMT, which recently listed on July 27. CXMT, in fact, outperforms Baidu, Alibaba, Tencent, and Xiaomi on a PE basis.
